title: Wills and Powers of Attorney
objectives: Inform clients about the advantages of a thoughtfully drafted will as a means of carrying out their wishes regarding the transfer of property at death and the control of some property after death.
Identify the circumstances where a substitute decision-maker may be needed.
Explain to clients the implications of appointing (or not appointing) an attorney for property and/or personal care.

guide.heading: Introduction and domicile
points: A will takes effect only on death and can be revoked any time before. It transfers legacies (bequests) to legatees and the residue (the balance of the net estate after debts, taxes and obligations) to the heirs.
Have it drafted by a lawyer (a notary in Quebec) with the planner's input: clear wording and stated reasons cut disputes, tax erosion, probate costs and lawsuits by disappointed heirs.
Common-law (de facto in Quebec) couples especially need wills: in some provinces intestacy law gives a common-law spouse nothing.

Formal validity is governed by the place the will is made or the testator's domicile: the one jurisdiction of strongest link plus intention to remain or return (home, family, bank accounts, work, social ties, visits, written intent).

Domicile where the will was executed governs administration; domicile at death decides which intestacy laws apply; real property follows the law where it is located. Residency, citizenship, domicile and mailing address are distinct.
The US levies estate tax on US-domiciled persons (green card holders included) and transfer taxes based on citizenship: ask early and refer to a US expert.

guide.heading: Holograph wills
points: Entirely handwritten by the testator (no typewriter or computer) and signed; witnesses are not needed. A signed letter showing testamentary intent can qualify.
Valid in AB, MB, NB, NL, ON, QC, SK, NWT and Yukon; BC accepts them only for moveable property (cash, stocks, bonds, jewellery).

Weaknesses: no professional advice (errors, misused legalese), easier to contest, hard to locate, no witness affidavit (the court needs, e.g., a bank manager to confirm the handwriting), and too many changes.
Undated, conflicting holographs (the 11-document example) lead to costly litigation over which ones govern.
Quebec: holograph wills must be probated by the court or a notary before use (art. 772 CCQ); recommended only when necessary, e.g., in an emergency.

guide.heading: Formal wills (made in the presence of witnesses)
points: Recognized in every province. Entirely in writing (by the testator or a third party) and signed by the testator before at least two witnesses, who sign in the testator's presence and in each other's.

Witnesses must be of the age of majority and should not be beneficiaries or beneficiaries' spouses: the will stays valid, but a witness-beneficiary's gift fails (some provinces allow court validation if there was no undue influence).
Have the witnesses swear an Affidavit of Execution at signing so the court can accept due execution without tracking them down years later.
Quebec: the testator declares to the witnesses that the will is his or hers; testator and witnesses initial every page (prudent elsewhere); the will must be probated by the court or a notary.
Kits and will software give no advice and miss tax planning: a last resort only, to be replaced by a professional will as soon as possible.

guide.heading: Notarial and international wills
points: Notarial wills exist only in Quebec: signed before one notary and, depending on the circumstances, one or two witnesses. The notary keeps the original; the testator gets a notarial copy.
As notarial deeds they are not probated; the notary issues certified copies to the heirs on proof of death. They can still be contested.
Witnesses cannot be the notary's spouse, the notary's relatives up to the third degree (direct or collateral, or by marriage or civil union), minors or the notary's employees.
Search reports from the Chamber of Notaries and the Quebec Bar reveal wills registered by notaries or lawyers. Outside Quebec, notaries mainly witness documents, swear affidavits and certify copies.

International wills follow a convention's uniform form and are valid wherever it applies, regardless of domicile, place signed or asset location; recognized (at writing) only in AB, MB, NL, NB, ON, PEI and SK.

guide.heading: Quebec: gift mortis causa in a marriage contract
points: A gift by spouses in a marriage or civil union contract, made with regard to the contingency of death (not its immediacy); it can take the place of a will.

Conditions: only in such a contract; donees limited to the future spouses and their respective and common children (born or unborn); no transfer of ownership; effective only at death; always revocable; signed by more than one person.
It stays valid for decades (made at 25, dies at 75 with no will: the spouse inherits). Always check the marriage contract when someone dies without a will.

guide.heading: Limits on testamentary freedom
points: Some assets can't be willed: property in joint tenancy with right of survivorship goes to the survivor; shares may be bound by a shareholders' agreement.
Forced heirship countries fix family shares by statute, so wills there may serve no purpose. Religious or cultural traditions may matter to clients but must be applied within Canadian law.
Situs wills: separate wills for each jurisdiction, often with different executors and beneficiaries.
Family law and support creditors don't challenge the will: they assert rights against the property and may rank ahead of beneficiaries. The will disposes of what is left after creditors and taxes.
Courts have limited power to fix technical errors; some provinces have 'substantial compliance' laws for minor violations if the document's integrity is not in question.

guide.heading: Testamentary capacity and undue influence
points: The testator must be of sound mind and acting freely. A declaration of competence in the will itself is not always reliable, and contests (incapacity, undue influence, fraud) can eat up the estate.
Incapacity is a later court judgment made with hindsight; the professional should inquire, keep notes or evidence (e.g., medical reports) and help clients exercise their right to make a will.
Each province sets a minimum age (sometimes waived, e.g., for married minors). Quebec: a person of full age under curatorship cannot make a will (art. 710).
Confirm the testator understands the assets, the beneficiaries, potential spouse or dependant claims and the will's terms.

Red flags: duress (bodily harm or threats); undue influence (unusual control by a third party, usually a beneficiary), e.g., a caregiver-beneficiary who books, attends and talks; a major unexplained change. Note concerns and tell the lawyer.

guide.heading: Family law and the surviving spouse
points: A will that fails to provide adequately for a spouse or dependants can be overridden. Cutting out a spouse isn't illegal, but dependants are creditors ranking ahead of beneficiaries, so it mostly breeds litigation.
Support orders or agreements generally bind the estate unless they release it (often on payment of life insurance in lieu of support).

Some provinces let a spouse choose will benefits or an equalization payment (some via Net Family Property). A successful claim generally forfeits all will benefits; the payment is received as a creditor.

Prevent claims by leaving the spouse more than the claim, often insurance-funded and 'in lieu of' statutory rights. Marriage contracts can waive equalization, but a spouse left without adequate resources may still claim support.
Quebec compensatory allowance (married or civil union spouses only) rests on having enriched the deceased with goods, services or money, not on need; the court decides.

Quebec family patrimony (residence, furniture, family car, RRSPs and RPPs accumulated during marriage): survivor may claim half unless renounced before July 1, 1989; partition comes before any distribution and can be added to will benefits.
Next the matrimonial regime is partitioned, and the spouse may also claim support. A Quebec will can make a legacy conditional on renouncing family patrimony rights.

guide.heading: Rights of other dependants and public policy
points: Dependants generally include spouses, common-law spouses, children (including unborn and born outside wedlock), grandchildren, parents, grandparents and siblings who were supported.

Quebec: only the married spouse, an ex-spouse owed support, the children and the parents can claim (arts. 684 to 695 CCQ); de facto spouses and siblings cannot. Support can be settled with the liquidator, or by court order.

Common-law three tests: was the deceased providing (or obliged to provide) support; did the deceased fail to provide adequately; is the dependant in need? Some provinces add the estate's ability to pay.

Courts weigh means and needs, lifetime gifts, the testator's written reasons and the accustomed lifestyle. BC's Wills Variation Act lets the court rewrite the will; Ontario can claw back non-estate assets such as insurance.
Discriminatory, illegal or public-policy-violating conditions can be struck: the gift may pass free of the condition or fail, at the estate's expense. Terror clauses are probably ineffective.

guide.heading: Revocation of a will
points: Revocable any time until death unless the testator becomes mentally incompetent. Most common: a new will with a revocation clause; also deliberate destruction by the testator, or in his or her presence under written instructions.
A later will without a revocation clause doesn't cancel the earlier one: the later prevails only where they conflict, so legacies in both may be paid.

Marriage revokes a will everywhere except Quebec, unless made in contemplation of that marriage (with a fallback if it doesn't happen); ON, NS and NB let the spouse elect to keep it. Quebec: the will stays valid.

Divorce doesn't revoke the whole will, but in QC, ON, BC, SK, MB and PEI gifts to and appointments of the ex-spouse are revoked. Legal separation has no effect except in BC. Any marital change merits a will review.

guide.heading: Review and amendment: codicils, memoranda, alterations
points: Review after material changes (estate value, liquidity, major assets, tax law, residence, births or deaths, health, marital status, relationships, family law) and every 3 to 5 years; an outdated will can be worse than none.

A codicil revokes, modifies or adds to a will and is executed like one (Quebec: same validity and probate rules). Prefer a new will for major changes like the residue or after many codicils; in Ontario beneficiaries see both.
A memorandum of personal items is binding only if it exists before the will is signed and is incorporated by reference; otherwise use a codicil.

Alterations and interlineations aren't allowed after signing; if made before, initial them (witnesses may bear the onus of proving timing). Obliterated words: the will stays valid as read. Quebec: initial every page.

guide.heading: Executors (liquidators): choice, fees and acceptance
points: Choose carefully: the executor (liquidator in Quebec) may manage large assets for years, and replacing one is long and costly.
A corporate executor (trust company) suits large estates or long trusts: experience, continuity, availability, impartiality (most valuable), multi-faceted expertise and financial security.

An individual suits small, simple estates and short trusts: likely to outlive the estate, financially skilled, reliable, knows the family. With co-executors (e.g., a trust company and the beneficiary), the will should say who breaks ties.

No alternate: if the executor dies mid-administration, his or her executor takes over; if the executor predeceases or declines, the court appoints an administrator. Quebec: heirs appoint a substitute liquidator, court as last resort.
Fees follow a court schedule (about 2.5% realized + 2.5% distributed + 5% of income), the same for any executor and paid by the estate; trust companies use compensation agreements.

Quebec: co-liquidators act unanimously (trustees by majority); a non-heir liquidator is paid, an heir only if the will or heirs agree; a sole-heir liquidator can't decline. Elsewhere an executor may decline before acting.

guide.heading: Guardians (tutors) and trustees
points: Wills in some provinces name a guardian for minors or disabled dependants; discuss it first and check funding. Common law: court approval, usually within 90 days, and the court can overrule in the children's best interests.
Quebec: parents designate a tutor (dative tutorship) by will, protection mandate or declaration to the Public Curator; no court step unless contested; not for disabled dependants.
Name trustees and alternates for any testamentary trust; the trustee can be the executor, spouse or guardian. In Quebec, a trust needs at least one independent (non-beneficiary) trustee.
Minors inheriting with no trustee: common law, the court appoints a public trustee until majority and the surviving parent has no automatic right; Quebec, the surviving parent is automatically tutor.

guide.heading: Drafting points: failed gifts, distribution and designations
points: Ademption: a specific gift fails if the asset is gone at death, with no replacement; use general wording.

Lapse: a gift to someone who predeceases falls into the residue; a lapsed residue causes a partial intestacy. Ontario anti-lapse: gifts to a child, grandchild or sibling pass to their family unless the will says 'if he survives me'.
Per stirpes ('by roots'): a predeceased child's share goes to his or her children; per capita (common law): survivors share equally. Quebec: representation (always per stirpes) and accretion.
Order: funeral costs, probate, legal and executor's fees, debts and taxes; then legacies; residue last. Legacies abate if the estate falls short, so the will should say how.
A survivorship clause (e.g., 30 days) avoids double administration after a common accident; don't attach it to the executor's appointment.

A will can name or revoke an insurance, RRSP or RRIF beneficiary (even an invalid will counts as a declaration); the later designation wins, but file it with the insurer. No irrevocable designation by will.
Usual clause order: revocation; executors and trustees; debts and taxes; legacies; residue; executor's powers; guardianship (tutorship); schedules or memoranda.

guide.heading: Powers of attorney for property and Quebec mandates
points: Without a power of attorney, incapacity forces a slow court application; not even a spouse can bind the other's property. PAs and living wills operate during life and end at death; a will acts only after death.

The grantor appoints an attorney (not necessarily a lawyer) over any property. An enduring or continuing PA must say it survives incapacity, or it ends when needed most. PAs also help with absence (vacation, broken leg).

Unless restricted, the attorney can do anything the grantor could except make or change a will; insurers generally say a PA can't change beneficiary designations. In Ontario a bank PA can accidentally revoke earlier general PAs.

Several attorneys act jointly (checks, but all must agree) or severally (flexible, no checks); name a substitute to avoid a court-appointed committee. A springing PA starts on a named person's declaration of incapacity.

Quebec: a simple mandate (power of attorney) covers property, takes effect when chosen and ends on incapacity or death. A protection mandate (notarial or before two disinterested witnesses) covers property and/or the person.

A protection mandate needs incapacity plus court homologation with medical and psychosocial evaluations (art. 2166), so 'enduring' doesn't exist in Quebec. A trust company may act for property but not the person.

Quebec endings: death, resignation (a protection mandatary must first find a substitute), a paid mandatary's bankruptcy, revocation, recovered capacity. The protection mandatary accounts to the heirs at the end, not to the Public Curator.

guide.heading: Personal care, court appointments and the planner's role
points: A PA for personal care covers housing, food, clothing and treatment consent; usable only once the grantor is incapable; never a corporate attorney. In Quebec the protection mandate can cover the person, even with different mandataries.

A 'living will' is generally not a legal document; an Advance Care Directive is a legal document consenting to or refusing treatment in advance. Consult a doctor, be specific and avoid 'no heroic measures'.

Clear directives must be followed by medical staff, but euthanasia instructions are unlikely to be followed. Treating against express wishes is the tort of battery. Quebec's 'biological will' states wishes but names no decision-maker.

If someone becomes incapable without a PA, family, friends or trust companies apply to the court or a government official; Quebec opens a protective regime with a tutor or curator, less flexible than a mandate.
Institutions may be liable for missing PA abuse. Planners should explain options rather than act as attorney (or witness the will), and document a client's growing confusion for family or the lawyer.

tips: EXAM TIP: In Quebec only notarial wills skip probate; holograph wills and wills made before witnesses must be probated by the court or a notary.
EXAM TIP: Marriage revokes a will everywhere except Quebec. In Quebec the will survives, but family patrimony and matrimonial regime rules come first.
EXAM TIP: A witness who is a beneficiary does not void the will; only the gift to that witness fails.
EXAM TIP: Two wills and no revocation clause? Both can stand; the later one wins only where they conflict.
EXAM TIP: An attorney for property can do almost anything the grantor could, except make, change or revoke the will.
DID YOU KNOW? Quebec has no 'enduring' power of attorney: a protection mandate works only after incapacity and court homologation.
EXAM TIP: A personal care power of attorney can be used only after the grantor becomes incapable, and never by a trust company.
DID YOU KNOW? In Quebec, de facto spouses and siblings cannot claim support from an estate; the married spouse, ex-spouse, children and parents can.
EXAM TIP: Leave 'my Buick' and sell it, and the gift adeems: the beneficiary gets nothing. 'My car' is safer.
DID YOU KNOW? A will can change a life insurance beneficiary, but the insurer may still pay whoever is on file unless it gets a copy.
EXAM TIP: Executor dies mid-job with no alternate? His executor steps in. Executor predeceased the testator? The court appoints an administrator.

flashcards.front: Testator, legacy (bequest), legatee and residue
flashcards.back: Testator: the person making the will. Legacy or bequest: a gift of cash or specific property. Legatee: the person receiving it. Residue: the balance of the net estate after debts, taxes and legacies, which goes to the residual heirs.

flashcards.front: Why common-law (de facto) couples especially need wills
flashcards.back: In some provinces, intestacy legislation does not provide for common-law spouses, so if the deceased has no will, the surviving common-law spouse may receive nothing.

flashcards.front: Domicile
flashcards.back: The jurisdiction with which a person has the strongest link and a present intention to remain (or return). A person may have several residences but only one domicile, established by facts and intentions.

flashcards.front: Factors used to establish domicile
flashcards.back: Location of the home; where the family lives; location of bank accounts and principal residence; regular employment; friends and social ties; frequency of visits to a previous domicile; written evidence of intention.

flashcards.front: Domicile at signing vs domicile at death vs location of real property
flashcards.back: Domicile where the will was executed: how the estate is administered. Domicile at death: which intestacy laws might apply. Real property: governed by the law of the place where it is located.

flashcards.front: Holograph will
flashcards.back: A will written entirely in the testator's own hand (no typewriter or computer) and signed by the testator, with or without witnesses. A letter declaring testamentary intent can qualify.

flashcards.front: Where holograph wills are valid
flashcards.back: AB, MB, NB, NL, ON, QC, SK, the NWT and Yukon. BC allows them only for moveable property (cash, stocks, bonds, jewellery).

flashcards.front: Weaknesses of holograph wills
flashcards.back: Usually made without professional advice (errors, omissions, misused legalese); more easily contested; often hard to locate; no witness affidavit, so harder to prove; easy to produce too many wills or changes.

flashcards.front: Which Quebec wills must be probated? (art. 772 CCQ)
flashcards.back: Holograph wills and wills made in the presence of witnesses, through the court or a notary, on the demand of any interested person, before they can be used. Notarial wills, being notarial deeds, are not probated.

flashcards.front: Formal (conventional) will requirements
flashcards.back: Entirely in writing (by the testator or a third party) and signed by the testator before at least two witnesses, who sign in the testator's presence and in each other's presence after the testator signs.

flashcards.front: Witness who is also a beneficiary
flashcards.back: A witness should be of the age of majority and should not be a beneficiary or a beneficiary's spouse. If a witness is a beneficiary, the will stays valid but that gift fails; some provinces let the court validate it if there was no undue influence.

flashcards.front: Affidavit of Execution
flashcards.back: Sworn by the witnesses when the will is signed. Once filed, the court can usually accept that the formalities were observed, with no need to find the witnesses at death. For an old will without one, a new will may be cheaper.

flashcards.front: Quebec will made in the presence of witnesses: extra formalities
flashcards.back: Before signing, the testator declares to the witnesses that the will is his or hers, and the testator and each witness initial every page (only prudent practice in common-law provinces). It must be probated before use.

flashcards.front: Do-it-yourself will kits and will software
flashcards.back: They produce documents without advice and don't handle complex situations or tax planning. Use only as a last resort when a professional will can't be obtained in time, and replace with a professional will as soon as possible.

flashcards.front: Notarial will (Quebec only)
flashcards.back: Signed before one notary and, depending on the circumstances, one or two witnesses. The notary keeps the original and the testator gets a notarial copy. Not probated, so certified copies go to heirs on proof of death; it can still be contested.

flashcards.front: How to find a will registered in Quebec
flashcards.back: Obtain search reports from the Chamber of Notaries and the Quebec Bar Association, which reveal wills registered by a notary or a lawyer. The same bodies can be searched for a protection mandate.

flashcards.front: Who cannot witness a Quebec notarial will
flashcards.back: The notary's spouse; the notary's relatives in the direct or collateral line up to and including the third degree, or connected by marriage or civil union; minors; and the notary's employees.

flashcards.front: International will
flashcards.back: Made under a convention providing a uniform law on form; valid wherever the convention is in force, regardless of domicile, place of signing or location of assets. Recognized (at writing) in AB, MB, NL, NB, ON, PEI and SK.

flashcards.front: Quebec gift mortis causa: conditions
flashcards.back: Only in a marriage or civil union contract, in place of a will; donees limited to the future spouses, their respective and common children (born or unborn); no transfer of ownership; effective at death; always revocable.

flashcards.front: Forced heirship jurisdiction
flashcards.back: A country whose statutes fix how much family members inherit, and no will can vary those rules. Like Canadian intestacy rules, but mandatory, so many residents there have no will.

flashcards.front: Situs wills
flashcards.back: Separate wills for each jurisdiction where a person has assets, often with different executors and different beneficiaries. They can also improve the confidentiality of the Canadian assets.

flashcards.front: 'Substantial compliance' law
flashcards.back: A law in some provinces that lets courts resolve minor technical violations in a will, as long as the integrity of the document is not in question.

flashcards.front: What the professional confirms the testator understands
flashcards.back: The assets that make up the estate; the persons who are to benefit; potential claims by a spouse or dependants; and the terms and conditions of the will. Also watch for duress or undue influence.

flashcards.front: Duress vs undue influence
flashcards.back: Duress: bodily harm or the threat of bodily harm. Undue influence: an unusual degree of control over the testator by a third party, usually a beneficiary under the proposed will.

flashcards.front: Minimum age to make a will
flashcards.back: Set by each province; some waive it in certain cases, such as a married minor. In Quebec, a person of full age under curatorship cannot make a will (art. 710 CCQ).

flashcards.front: Dependants' relief legislation
flashcards.back: Ensures adequate support for spouses and other financial dependants when someone dies, with or without a will. Dependants (spouses, common-law spouses, children, parents, siblings) can ask the court to modify the will.

flashcards.front: Quebec: who can claim support from an estate
flashcards.back: Only the married spouse, an ex-spouse who was owed support, the children and the parents (arts. 684 to 695 CCQ). De facto spouses and brothers and sisters are not dependants for support claims.

flashcards.front: Equalization claim (some common-law provinces)
flashcards.back: The surviving spouse takes either the benefits under the will or an equalization payment from the estate. If the claim succeeds, will benefits are generally forfeited and the payment is received as a creditor.

flashcards.front: Quebec compensatory allowance
flashcards.back: A claim by a married or civil union spouse based on having enriched the deceased through goods, services or money, not on need. The court decides whether it applies.

flashcards.front: Quebec family patrimony on death
flashcards.back: Principal residence, furniture, a family automobile, and RRSPs and RPPs accumulated during the marriage. The survivor may claim half (unless renounced before July 1, 1989) before any distribution; the matrimonial regime is partitioned next.

flashcards.front: Keeping a spouse from claiming against the estate
flashcards.back: Leave the spouse more by will (often funded by life insurance) than the claim is worth, stated to be in lieu of statutory rights. In Quebec, make the legacy conditional on renouncing family patrimony rights.

flashcards.front: Three tests for awarding support to a dependant (common law)
flashcards.back: 1) Was the deceased providing, or obliged to provide, support? 2) Did the deceased fail to provide adequately, by will or otherwise? 3) Is the dependant in need of support? Some provinces also weigh the estate's ability to pay.

flashcards.front: Who counts as a child for dependants' relief
flashcards.back: Includes a child unborn at the date of death (or marriage breakdown) and children born outside of wedlock. Other dependants can include grandchildren, parents, grandparents and siblings who were supported.

flashcards.front: BC Wills Variation Act vs Ontario clawback
flashcards.back: BC: the court can, in effect, rewrite the will to meet unfulfilled obligations. Ontario: even property passing outside the will, like insurance payable to a named beneficiary, can be clawed back to assess support.

flashcards.front: Will conditions that can be struck down
flashcards.back: Conditions contrary to public policy, promoting an illegal act, or discriminatory (e.g., forfeiting a gift for marrying outside a race or joining a religious order). The gift may pass free of the condition or fail; terror clauses rarely work.

flashcards.front: Ways to revoke a will
flashcards.back: Most commonly a later will with a revocation clause ('I hereby revoke all my former wills and codicils'); or deliberate destruction by the testator, or in his or her presence and under written instructions. Not once mentally incompetent.

flashcards.front: Later will with no revocation clause
flashcards.back: Both wills may be valid. Where they conflict (e.g., the residue), the later will prevails; where they don't (e.g., separate cash legacies), both apply, so legacies under both may be payable.

flashcards.front: Effect of marriage on an existing will
flashcards.back: Revokes it in every province except Quebec, unless made in contemplation of that marriage (ON, NS and NB let the spouse elect to keep it). In Quebec the will stays valid, subject to family patrimony and matrimonial regime rules.

flashcards.front: Effect of divorce and legal separation on a will
flashcards.back: Divorce: gifts to and appointments of the ex-spouse are revoked in QC and in ON, BC, SK, MB and PEI (where the ex-spouse is presumed to have predeceased). Legal separation: no effect in most provinces; BC treats it like divorce.

flashcards.front: Codicil
flashcards.back: A document that revokes, modifies or adds to a will without redrafting it; attached to the will and executed like one (in Quebec, same validity and probate conditions). Use a new will for major changes like the residue or after many codicils.

flashcards.front: Memorandum of personal items
flashcards.back: A list of items and recipients kept with the will. Legally binding only if it existed before the will was signed and is incorporated by reference; otherwise use a codicil to make the wishes binding.

flashcards.front: Alterations, interlineations and obliterations
flashcards.back: Alterations (changes) and interlineations (words inserted between lines) aren't allowed after signing; if made before, the testator and witnesses initial them nearby. Obliterated words: the will stays valid, and readable words form it.

flashcards.front: Advantages of a corporate executor (trust company)
flashcards.back: Experience, continuity, attention and availability, impartiality (the most intangible but most valuable), multi-faceted expertise and financial security ('deep pockets'). Best for large estates or long-lasting trusts.

flashcards.front: When an individual executor is appropriate
flashcards.back: Small estate, simple assets, short-lived trusts (e.g., an education trust for minors). The person should be likely to outlive the estate, know finance, tax and investing, be reliable and available, and know the testator's wishes.

flashcards.front: No alternate executor named: what happens
flashcards.back: Executor dies mid-administration: the executor's executor is automatically appointed. Named executor predeceases the testator or won't serve: the court appoints an administrator. Quebec: the heirs appoint a substitute liquidator; court as last resort.

flashcards.front: Quebec liquidator rules
flashcards.back: Co-liquidators act unanimously (trustees by majority). A liquidator who is not an heir is compensated; an heir-liquidator is not, unless the will or the heirs provide it. A liquidator who is the sole heir cannot decline the office.

flashcards.front: Guardian named in a will (common-law provinces)
flashcards.back: The clause only states the testator's wishes: the guardian must be approved by court order, usually within the first 90 days, and the court may overrule the choice in the children's best interests.

flashcards.front: Quebec tutor designated by parents (dative tutorship)
flashcards.back: Parents can designate a tutor for minor children by will, protection mandate or a declaration sent to the Public Curator; no court proceeding unless contested for serious reasons. Not available for disabled dependants.

flashcards.front: Minor inherits and no trustee is named
flashcards.back: Common law: the court appoints a public trustee until majority; the surviving parent has no automatic right to manage it. Quebec: the surviving parent is automatically tutor and administers the legacy under tutorship rules.

flashcards.front: Ademption
flashcards.back: Failure of a gift of a specific asset that the testator no longer owns at death (sold, lost, destroyed or converted). No replacement is given, even if traceable; general wording ('my car', not 'my Buick') helps.

flashcards.front: Lapse, partial intestacy and anti-lapse
flashcards.back: A gift to someone who predeceases lapses into the residue; if the residuary heir predeceases, a partial intestacy results. Anti-lapse (e.g., Ontario): gifts to a child, grandchild or sibling go to their family unless 'if he survives me'.

flashcards.front: Quebec: representation vs accretion
flashcards.back: Representation: a descendant inherits in place of a predeceased beneficiary of a residual legacy (or intestate heir), unless the will says otherwise. Accretion: cottage left to A and B; A dies before the testator, so B takes it all.

flashcards.front: Per stirpes vs per capita
flashcards.back: Per stirpes ('by roots'): a predeceased beneficiary's share goes to his or her children. Per capita (common law): only surviving beneficiaries share, equally. In Quebec, devolution by representation is always per stirpes.

flashcards.front: Order of distribution of an estate
flashcards.back: Funeral expenses, probate fees, legal and executor's fees, debts and taxes come first; then general and specific legacies; the residue is distributed last.

flashcards.front: Abatement
flashcards.back: Reducing legacies when debts, taxes and expenses exceed expectations, proportionately or not. Example: three $10,000 legacies but only $20,000 left gives each child about $6,666. The will should say how abatement is shared.

flashcards.front: Survivorship clause
flashcards.back: Names an alternate beneficiary if the primary one doesn't survive the testator by a set period (e.g., 30 days), so assets aren't administered twice after a common accident. Don't tie the executor's appointment to it.

flashcards.front: Naming an insurance, RRSP or RRIF beneficiary in a will
flashcards.back: Allowed (subject to local rules); even an invalid will counts as a written declaration. The later designation prevails, but file the will or a new form with the insurer. A will cannot make an irrevocable designation.

flashcards.front: Normal order of clauses in a will
flashcards.back: Revocation; appointment of executors and trustees; payment of debts, taxes and expenses; legacies; residue; executor's powers; guardianship (tutorship) of minors; attached schedules or memoranda.

flashcards.front: Incapacity without a power of attorney
flashcards.back: No one has automatic authority, not even a spouse. A family member must make a time-consuming court application, and meanwhile no one can manage the assets (e.g., trade a brokerage account).

flashcards.front: Quebec simple mandate (power of attorney)
flashcards.back: Covers the administration of property only; takes effect when the grantor chooses (e.g., on signature); revocable at any time; ends on the mandator's incapacity or death. The mandatary accounts to the grantor.

flashcards.front: Quebec protection mandate
flashcards.back: Made by a capable mandator by notarial act or before two witnesses with no interest, naming a mandatary for property and/or the person. Executed only after incapacity and court homologation (art. 2166 CCQ). A trust company can't act for the person.

flashcards.front: Enduring (continuing) power of attorney
flashcards.back: A property power of attorney that expressly continues during the grantor's mental incapacity; without that wording it ceases on incapacity. The concept doesn't exist in Quebec, where a mandate needs homologation.

flashcards.front: What an attorney for property cannot do
flashcards.back: Make, change or revoke the grantor's will. Otherwise, unless restricted, the attorney can do almost anything the grantor could. Insurers generally hold that a PA for property may not affect beneficiary designations.

flashcards.front: Joint vs several attorneys
flashcards.back: Joint: all must agree, giving checks and balances, but all must be available (risk of deadlock). Several: each can act alone, which is flexible but has no checks. Corporate attorneys accept joint but prefer not several.

flashcards.front: Springing (contingent) power of attorney
flashcards.back: Takes effect only when an independent person named in it (e.g., the family doctor) declares the grantor incapable; third parties accept it once they receive that declaration. Most powers of attorney take effect on signing.

flashcards.front: Quebec: how a power of attorney or protection mandate ends
flashcards.back: Mandator's death; resignation (a protection mandatary must first find a substitute); a paid mandatary's bankruptcy; revocation by the mandator (simple mandate); the mandator regains capacity (protection ends).

flashcards.front: Attorney's accountability after the grantor's incapacity
flashcards.back: Common law: the attorney becomes accountable to the court. Quebec protection mandate: the mandatary accounts to the heirs at the end, with no periodic accounting to the Public Curator. Simple mandate: to the grantor.

flashcards.front: Power of attorney for personal care
flashcards.back: Lets a substitute decide on living arrangements, food, clothing and consent to treatment. Usable only once the grantor is mentally incapable; cannot be given to a corporate attorney. In Quebec, the protection mandate covers this.

flashcards.front: Living will vs Advance Care Directive
flashcards.back: Living will: in most provinces not a legal document, just wishes about future medical care. Advance Care Directive (Advance Healthcare Directive): a legal document consenting to, or refusing, treatment in advance of need.

flashcards.front: Quebec 'biological will'
flashcards.back: A simple document in which the grantor describes his or her wishes about treatment. Unlike a protection mandate, it does not designate anyone to make decisions in his or her place.

flashcards.front: Quebec protective regime
flashcards.back: If an incapable person has no protection mandate, any interested person can ask the court to open a protective regime and appoint a tutor or curator: similar authority, but less flexible and without the person's own directions.

flashcards.front: Financial planner's role with powers of attorney
flashcards.back: Explain the advantages and risks of the options rather than act as the attorney. Watch for abuse of powers of attorney (institutions can be liable), and document a client's growing confusion for the family or lawyer.

flashcards.front: Executor compensation rule of thumb
flashcards.back: About 2.5% of assets realized + 2.5% of assets distributed + 5% of estate income (court schedule), plus possible ongoing fees. Same whether a trust company, lawyer or relative acts; paid by the estate.

flashcards.front: How often to review a will
flashcards.back: Whenever material changes occur, and periodically: about every 3 to 5 years.

flashcards.front: Typical survivorship period in a will
flashcards.back: 30 days, kept short because the beneficiaries are uncertain until the period ends.

flashcards.front: Time limit for court approval of a guardian named in a will
flashcards.back: Usually within the first 90 days (common-law provinces).

flashcards.front: Witnesses needed for each type of will
flashcards.back: Formal will: at least two, of the age of majority. Holograph will: none. Quebec notarial will: one notary plus one or two witnesses, depending on the circumstances.

questions.q: According to the course, which law generally governs a testator's real property, such as land and buildings?
options: The law of the province where the executor lives
The law of the place where the will was signed
The law of the testator's domicile at the time of death
The law of the place where the real property is located
questions.explain: Real property is governed by the laws of the place where it is located. By contrast, the domicile where the will was executed determines how the estate is administered, and the domicile at death determines which intestacy laws might apply.

questions.q: Lise lived and worked in Quebec all her life; her family, friends and bank accounts are there, and she signed her will there. In retirement she wintered at a condo in Nova Scotia and died there in March. What is most likely her domicile?
options: Quebec, because her life and connections were centred there
Both provinces, so each one's law governs half of her estate
Nova Scotia, because she was residing there when she died
Whichever province her executor chooses when applying for probate
questions.explain: A person may have several residences but only one domicile: the place of strongest connection, established by facts (home, family, bank accounts, work, friends) and intentions. Where she happened to be living at death does not override a life centred in Quebec.

questions.q: A Canadian resident who holds a US green card may have trouble avoiding US estate tax, because the US taxes persons domiciled there regardless of where they are temporarily resident at death.
options: True
False
questions.explain: True. The US imposes estate tax on persons domiciled there, and a green card holder would have great difficulty denying US domicile. The US also taxes transfers based on citizenship, so planners should ask about both early and refer to a US expert.

questions.q: What makes a will a holograph will?
options: It is handwritten by a friend of the testator and then signed before a notary
It is typed by the testator and then signed by him or her before two adult witnesses
It is entirely handwritten and signed by the testator, with or without witnesses
It is completed on a pre-printed kit form and signed by the testator alone
questions.explain: A holograph will is written entirely in the testator's own hand, with no typewriter or computer, and signed by the testator; witnesses are not required. A typed will signed before two witnesses is a formal (witnessed) will.

questions.q: Which statement about where holograph wills are recognized is accurate, according to the course?
options: British Columbia accepts them only for moveable property, such as cash and stocks
They are valid in every Canadian province and territory, with no exceptions at all
Ontario does not accept them, because every Ontario will needs two adult witnesses
Quebec does not accept them, because every Quebec will must be signed before a notary
questions.explain: Holograph wills are valid in AB, MB, NB, NL, ON, QC, SK, the NWT and Yukon, while BC allows them only for moveable property. Because the rules vary, check the rules of the home province or of the place where the assets are located.

questions.q: In Quebec, a holograph will can be used to settle the estate as soon as the testator dies, without any probate by the court or a notary.
options: True
False
questions.explain: False. In Quebec, a holograph will (like a will made in the presence of witnesses) must be probated through the court or a notary, on the demand of any interested person, before it can be used (art. 772 CCQ). Only notarial wills avoid probate.

questions.q: Over two years, Edgar wrote nine handwritten wills, each signed and each showing testamentary intent, but he dated none of them. Several conflict with one another. What is the most likely result after his death?
options: All nine are void, because holograph wills must be signed before witnesses
His estate passes on intestacy, because undated wills are always ignored
The last one found in his desk automatically revokes all of the others
Costly litigation to decide which documents govern and how they fit together
questions.explain: Each signed, handwritten document expressing testamentary intent can be a valid holograph will, even if they conflict. With no dates, no one can tell which came last, so the heirs face expensive litigation, as in the course's example of the bachelor who saved on legal fees.

questions.q: In a common-law province, which signing procedure meets the requirements for a formal (witnessed) will?
options: Typed will; testator signs before two witnesses, who then sign in each other's presence
Typed will; testator and two witnesses initial every page, then a notary signs it as well
Typed will; testator signs alone, then two witnesses sign a later declaration
Handwritten will; testator signs, and one adult witness signs the next day
questions.explain: A formal will must be entirely in writing (by the testator or a third party) and signed by the testator before at least two witnesses, who sign in the testator's presence and in each other's. Initialling every page is required in Quebec but only prudent elsewhere.

questions.q: Raj's formal will leaves $20,000 to his neighbour Tom and the residue to Raj's children. Tom was one of the two witnesses who signed the will. In a common-law province, what is the general result?
options: The whole will is void, and the estate passes on intestacy
The will stands, and Tom's gift is valid since he is an adult
The will stands, but the $20,000 gift to Tom is invalid
The will stands only if a third witness confirms the signature
questions.explain: A will remains valid when a witness is a beneficiary, but the gift to that witness fails. In some provinces the witness-beneficiary may ask the court to validate the gift by proving the testator was not under his or her undue influence.

questions.q: Monique, in Quebec, signs a typed will in the presence of two adult witnesses. Which formality is required by law in Quebec but considered only prudent practice in the common-law provinces?
options: A notary countersigns the will after the witnesses have signed it
The will is registered with the Public Curator within 90 days
The testator and each witness initial every page of the will
The witnesses are relatives of the testator up to the third degree
questions.explain: In Quebec, the testator declares to the witnesses that the will is his or hers, and the testator and each witness initial every page. Common-law provinces don't require initialling but consider it prudent. A Quebec will made before witnesses still needs probate.

questions.q: Which pairing of a will type with its execution requirements is correct?
options: Notarial will: signed before two notaries, with no witnesses ever required
Quebec will made before witnesses: typed, signed before a single witness
Holograph will: in the testator's handwriting, and two witnesses must sign
Formal will: in writing by anyone, signed by the testator before two witnesses
questions.explain: A formal will may be written by the testator or a third party but must be signed before at least two witnesses. A holograph will needs no witnesses, and a notarial will is signed before one notary plus, depending on circumstances, one or two witnesses.

questions.q: Which feature sets a Quebec notarial will apart from a holograph will or a will made in the presence of witnesses?
options: As a notarial deed it is not probated; certified copies issue without proceedings
It can no longer be contested once the notary issues certified copies to the heirs
It must be handwritten by the testator and kept at home until the testator's death
It must be signed before three witnesses and then probated by the Superior Court
questions.explain: Notarial wills are notarial deeds, so they are not subject to probate: the notary keeps the original and issues certified copies to the heirs on proof of death. Escaping probate does not mean a notarial will cannot be contested.

questions.q: Which of these people could act as a witness to a Quebec notarial will?
options: The notary's adult legal assistant, who works full time in the notary's own office
The notary's 17-year-old son, who happens to be visiting the office that day
The notary's adult brother, who has no connection at all to the testator
The testator's adult neighbour, who is not related to or employed by the notary
questions.explain: A witness to a notarial will cannot be the notary's spouse, a relative of the notary in the direct or collateral line up to the third degree (a brother falls within this), a relative by marriage or civil union, a minor, or the notary's employee.

questions.q: Manfred, 79 and increasingly forgetful, asks his financial planner to witness the new will he is preparing with a store-bought kit. What is the best response?
options: Agree to witness, since a planner is a neutral adult with nothing to gain
Agree to witness, as long as a second witness signs on the same occasion
Decline, because a kit will is valid only if written entirely by hand
Decline to witness, and urge him to have a lawyer or notary prepare the will
questions.explain: The planner should stay objective and apart from the documentation of the client's estate plan, so should not witness. Kit wills come with no advice, and given possible capacity and undue influence issues, Manfred should get advice from a lawyer (or a notary).

questions.q: Which statement about international wills is accurate, according to the course?
options: They are valid wherever the convention is in force, whatever the testator's domicile
They are valid only where the testator was domiciled when the will was signed
Every Canadian province and territory had recognized them by the time of writing the course
Quebec recognizes them, since it already uses notarial wills for most estates
questions.explain: An international will follows a convention's uniform law on form, so it is valid wherever the convention is in force, regardless of domicile, place of signing or location of assets. At the time of writing only AB, MB, NL, NB, ON, PEI and SK recognized it, not Quebec.

questions.q: In Quebec, what is a gift mortis causa?
options: A gift made during life that transfers ownership to a child immediately
A gift handed over in person by someone who expects to die from an illness within days
A gift in a marriage or civil union contract that takes effect at the donor's death
A gift set out in a handwritten codicil later attached to a notarial will
questions.explain: In Quebec, a gift mortis causa is made by spouses in their marriage or civil union contract with regard to the contingency of death, not its immediacy. It can take the place of a will, so the contract should be checked when someone dies without a will.

questions.q: Which statement about a gift mortis causa in a Quebec marriage contract is accurate?
options: It becomes irrevocable once both spouses sign the notarial marriage contract
It is always revocable, and no ownership is transferred during the donor's life
It must be confirmed in a later will, or it lapses at the donor's death
It may benefit anyone the donor chooses, including friends and charities
questions.explain: The gift is always revocable, like any will; there is no actual transfer of ownership, and it takes effect only at the donor's death. Donees are limited to the future spouses, their respective children and their common children, born or unborn.

questions.q: In a common-law province, which asset passes outside the will rather than under it?
options: Real estate held in joint tenancy with right of survivorship
A cottage owned solely by the testator at the date of death
Personal effects such as jewellery, furniture and a vehicle
A non-registered investment account in the testator's sole name
questions.explain: Property held as joint tenants with right of survivorship goes to the surviving joint tenant, not under the will. Other assets may be restricted by prior contracts, such as shares covered by a shareholders' agreement.

questions.q: When a family law or support creditor makes a claim against an estate, the creditor is challenging the validity of the will.
options: True
False
questions.explain: False. Family law and support creditors are not challenging the will; they are exerting other rights against the deceased's property, and they may rank ahead of the beneficiaries. Whatever is left after creditors and tax authorities are paid passes under the will.

questions.q: While taking will instructions, which situation should most concern the professional as a sign of possible undue influence?
options: A caregiver-beneficiary booked the meeting, attends it and answers for the testator
The testator asks to name a trust company as executor instead of a close family member
The testator brings a list of assets that her accountant prepared for the meeting
The testator wants equal shares for her children, just as in her previous will
questions.explain: Undue influence is an unusual degree of control by a third party, usually a beneficiary. A dependent testator whose caregiver-beneficiary arranges the appointment, attends and does most of the talking is a warning sign, as is a major unexplained change from earlier wills.

questions.q: Under article 710 of the Civil Code of Quebec, who cannot make a will?
options: A person of full age who is under curatorship
A person who made a gift mortis causa in a marriage contract
A person aged 18 to 21 who has never been married
A person of full age who has signed a protection mandate
questions.explain: Article 710 says a person of full age under curatorship cannot make a will. Elsewhere, each province sets a minimum age, which some provinces waive in certain cases, such as for a married minor.

questions.q: According to the course, what is the will-drafting professional's role regarding a client's mental capacity?
options: Certify the client's capacity in writing, which makes the will unchallengeable
Inquire and keep notes or other evidence so a court can later rule on validity
Refuse instructions from any client over 75 who lacks a recent medical report
Rely on a clause in the will in which the client declares that he is competent
questions.explain: Strictly, deciding capacity is not the drafter's job: incapacity is a later court judgment made with hindsight. The professional should inquire and record notes or gather evidence (e.g., medical reports); a self-declaration of competence in the will is not always reliable.

questions.q: Manfred plans a new will that leaves nothing to his wife, who now lives in a nursing home, and names his son Hans as primary beneficiary. What should he be told?
options: He may disinherit her, since spouses who live apart lose all of their rights to the estate
She can claim only if the will is a holograph will rather than a formal will
The will is illegal and void, so the estate would pass under the intestacy rules
His wife will still have property and possibly support rights that must be considered
questions.explain: A will that cuts out a spouse is not invalid or illegal, but it cannot defeat her rights: spouses and dependants have property and support rights under provincial law that rank ahead of beneficiaries, and ignoring them invites costly litigation.

questions.q: In Quebec, which group lists only people who can claim support from a deceased person's estate?
options: Married or de facto spouse, children, parents and grandparents
Married spouse, de facto spouse, children and brothers and sisters
Children, grandchildren, brothers and sisters, and de facto spouse
Married spouse, ex-spouse owed support, children and parents
questions.explain: In Quebec, only the married spouse, an ex-spouse to whom the deceased owed support, the children and the parents can claim (arts. 684 to 695 CCQ). De facto spouses and brothers and sisters are not dependants for support purposes, unlike in many common-law provinces.

questions.q: In Quebec, on what basis does a surviving spouse claim a compensatory allowance from the estate?
options: The spouse contributed goods, services or money that enriched the deceased
The spouse lived with the deceased in a de facto union for over three years
The spouse lacks the income to keep the lifestyle the couple had enjoyed
The spouse received less under the will than half of the family patrimony
questions.explain: A compensatory allowance is not based on need: it rests on the survivor having enriched the deceased through goods, services or money, and the court decides whether it applies. Only legally married or civil union spouses can claim it, not de facto spouses.

questions.q: Which asset belongs to the Quebec family patrimony as described in the course?
options: Savings held in one spouse's personal chequing account
RRSPs and RPP benefits accumulated during the marriage
Shares of a private company owned by one of the spouses
A non-registered stock portfolio held by one of the spouses
questions.explain: The course lists the family patrimony as the principal residence, the furniture, a family automobile, and RRSPs and RPPs accumulated during the marriage. On death, the surviving spouse can claim half of it before any distribution to beneficiaries.

questions.q: Which statement about partition of the family patrimony when a Quebec marriage ends by death is accurate?
options: It applies only if the will is silent, since a will can cancel the spouse's share
It applies only to couples married after July 1, 1989 under separation of property
It is made before any distribution and can be added to benefits under the will
It is made after the legacies are paid, out of whatever residue remains
questions.explain: The partition must be made before any distribution to beneficiaries, and the survivor can claim it in addition to benefits under the will (absent particular provisions) or intestacy, unless rights were renounced before July 1, 1989. Partition of the matrimonial regime follows.

questions.q: Hector, in a common-law province, wants his second wife Mira to accept his will rather than claim against his assets under matrimonial property law, so his children can inherit the rest. Her claim would be worth about $250,000. Which plan does the course favour?
options: Name Mira beneficiary of a $250,000 policy and leave the whole estate to the children
Leave Mira $200,000 by will, with a clause forbidding any claim under the statute
Leave Mira $300,000 by will, funded by insurance, in lieu of her statutory rights
Leave Mira nothing and add a clause disinheriting anyone who contests the will
questions.explain: Make taking under the will more attractive than claiming: leave a legacy greater than the claim (often funded by life insurance), stated to be in lieu of statutory rights. Clauses penalizing challengers are probably ineffective, and in some provinces insurance paid by designation may not offset the claim.

questions.q: If a spouse gave up an equalization claim in a marriage contract, that spouse can never claim support from the estate, even if left without adequate resources.
options: True
False
questions.explain: False. Spouses may agree in a marriage contract to forgo statutory rights such as an equalization claim, but a surviving spouse who has not been left adequate resources to live on often may still make a claim for support despite the contract.

questions.q: In a common-law province, a court is deciding whether to award support from an estate to the deceased's adult daughter. Which question is one of the three usual tests?
options: Is the daughter named as a residual beneficiary?
Was the daughter living in the deceased's home?
Did the daughter contest the will within 30 days?
Is the daughter in need of support?
questions.explain: The three tests: was the deceased providing (or obliged to provide) support; did the deceased fail to provide adequately, by will or otherwise; and is the dependant in need of support. Some provinces also consider the estate's ability to pay.

questions.q: How does British Columbia's Wills Variation Act differ from the Ontario approach described in the course?
options: BC courts can rewrite the will; Ontario can claw back some non-estate assets
BC covers only spouses; Ontario covers only minor and disabled children
BC lets claimants seize insurance; Ontario forbids any variation of a will
BC courts can only award cash; Ontario courts can rewrite the will itself
questions.explain: Under BC's Wills Variation Act, the court can in effect rewrite the will to meet unfulfilled obligations. In Ontario, even property passing outside the will, such as life insurance payable to a named beneficiary, can be clawed back into the estate to assess support.

questions.q: When setting support for a dependant, a court may consider the testator's written reasons for leaving that dependant out of the will.
options: True
False
questions.explain: True. Courts consider the dependant's means and needs, gifts or provisions made during the deceased's life, the testator's written reasons for depriving a dependant, and the lifestyle the dependant was accustomed to.

questions.q: Which will condition is most likely to be challenged as contrary to public policy?
options: A nephew's gift is held in trust until he reaches the age of 25
A charity's gift must be used only to fund its scholarship program
A niece forfeits her gift if she marries a person of a certain race
A son's gift depends on his surviving the testator by 30 days
questions.explain: A will cannot set conditions that are discriminatory, contrary to public policy or that promote an illegal act. Age-based trusts, restricted charitable gifts and survivorship conditions are ordinary planning tools.

questions.q: Nadia's formal will leaves the residue to her husband and $10,000 to a hospital. Years later she writes a valid holograph will leaving $10,000 to a library; it has no revocation clause and says nothing about the residue. What is the likely result?
options: Both wills may stand: the husband takes the residue and both legacies are paid
The new will revokes the old one, so only the library legacy is valid
The formal will governs, because a holograph will cannot alter a formal will
Both wills are void, because two wills cannot exist at the same time
questions.explain: A later will without a revocation clause does not automatically revoke an earlier one. Where the wills conflict, the later prevails; where they don't (such as separate cash legacies), both can be valid, so both $10,000 legacies may be payable.

questions.q: Sophie (Quebec) and Liam (Manitoba) each made a will while single, not in contemplation of marriage. Both later married without making new wills. What is the status of their wills?
options: Sophie's will remains valid; Liam's was revoked by his marriage
Both wills were revoked by marriage, so both would die intestate
Both wills remain valid, subject only to family law claims
Liam's will remains valid; Sophie's was revoked by her marriage
questions.explain: Outside Quebec, a later marriage revokes a will unless it was made in contemplation of that marriage (ON, NS and NB let the spouse elect to keep it). In Quebec, a will made before marriage stays valid, though family patrimony and matrimonial regime rules apply first.

questions.q: Which statement about the effect of divorce or legal separation on a will is accurate?
options: In Quebec, divorce revokes legacies to the ex-spouse and the ex-spouse's role as liquidator
In Quebec, divorce revokes the entire will, so a new will must be drawn up right away to avoid intestacy
In most provinces, legal separation revokes all gifts to the estranged spouse
In British Columbia, divorce affects a will, but legal separation never does
questions.explain: Divorce doesn't generally revoke a will, but in Quebec (and ON, BC, SK, MB and PEI) gifts to and appointments of the former spouse are revoked. Legal separation has no effect in most provinces; BC is the only province that treats it like divorce.

questions.q: A will can be revoked at any time before death, even after the testator has become mentally incompetent.
options: True
False
questions.explain: False. A will takes effect only on death and can be revoked at any time before then, unless the testator becomes mentally incompetent, in which case it can no longer be revoked.

questions.q: Apart from reviewing a will after major life events, how often does the course suggest a periodic review?
options: About every 3 to 5 years
About once every year
Only when tax laws change
About every 10 to 15 years
questions.explain: Wills should be reviewed whenever material changes occur and periodically, say every 3 to 5 years, since small changes add up. An outdated will can sometimes be worse than no will at all.

questions.q: An Ontario client wants to shift most of her estate from her nieces, who don't know her will's contents, to charities. Why might a new will be better than a codicil?
options: A codicil is valid only if a notary signs it within 30 days of the will
With a codicil, the nieces would see the original will and learn it was changed
A codicil cannot change the residue of an estate, since it is not executed like a will
A codicil would revoke the whole original will and cause an intestacy
questions.explain: Codicils are executed like wills but aren't recommended for major changes such as the residue. In provinces like Ontario, beneficiaries receive copies of the old will and the codicil, so a new will avoids revealing (and hurting with) the change.

questions.q: For a memorandum listing personal items and who should receive them to be legally binding, what is required?
options: It must be approved by the liquidator and filed with the court before death
It must be signed by two witnesses each time an item is added or removed
It must exist before the will is signed and be incorporated by reference
It must be handwritten by the testator and dated after the will is signed
questions.explain: A memorandum is binding only if it exists before the will is signed and is incorporated by reference. A list drawn up later isn't binding (families often honour it anyway); to make later wishes binding, the testator can use a codicil.

questions.q: After a will was signed, some of its words were blacked out so they can no longer be read. What is the effect?
options: The will is valid only if the testator initialled the blacked-out words
The whole will is revoked, because it was altered after being signed
The will is still valid, and the words that remain readable form the will
The court restores the original words using the lawyer's draft copy
questions.explain: Words deleted or erased so they can't be read are obliterations: the will remains valid and whatever is still readable constitutes it. Alterations and interlineations aren't permitted after signing; changes made before signing should be initialled by the testator and witnesses.

questions.q: Manfred, 79, plans to name his brother Fritz, 71, as executor. His will creates trusts for his minor grandchildren that last until they turn 30. What is the best advice?
options: Keep Fritz, since a poor executor can easily be replaced later at little cost
Keep Fritz, since the court fee schedule is lower when a relative does the work
Keep Fritz, since a relative always knows the family better than a trust company
Consider a younger executor or a corporate trustee, as the trusts may last decades
questions.explain: An executor and trustee should be likely to outlive the estate and any trusts. With trusts that may run for years or decades, a younger person or a corporate trustee is more prudent. Replacing an executor later is long and expensive, and fees follow the same schedule for all.

questions.q: In a common-law province, Ruth's will names Ken as sole executor, with no alternate. Ken dies partway through administering Ruth's estate. Who takes over?
options: The Public Trustee automatically takes over the administration
Ruth's residual heirs must agree unanimously on a new executor
The court appoints an administrator, since no alternate was named
Ken's own executor is automatically appointed to finish the job
questions.explain: Without an alternate, if the executor dies before the estate is fully administered, the executor's executor is automatically appointed. If the named executor predeceases the testator or won't serve, the court appoints an administrator. In Quebec, the heirs appoint a substitute liquidator.

questions.q: Which statement about liquidators in Quebec is accurate?
options: A liquidator who is also an heir is always entitled to be paid by the estate
A liquidator who is the sole heir may decline the office before starting to act
Co-liquidators must act unanimously; trustees act by majority unless otherwise provided
Co-liquidators act by majority vote, while trustees must always act unanimously on every decision
questions.explain: In Quebec, several liquidators must agree unanimously, while trustees act by majority unless otherwise provided. A liquidator who is the sole heir cannot decline the office, and an heir-liquidator has no right to remuneration unless the will or the heirs provide for it.

questions.q: Using the course's rough guideline for executor fees, estimate the compensation on an estate that realizes $400,000 of assets, distributes $400,000 and earns $20,000 of income during administration.
questions.explain: 2.5% of $400,000 realized ($10,000) + 2.5% of $400,000 distributed ($10,000) + 5% of $20,000 income ($1,000) = about $21,000, paid by the estate. The schedule is the same whether the executor is a trust company, a lawyer or a family member.

questions.q: Dana is named executor of her uncle's estate, which includes a factory facing environmental claims. In a common-law province, which statement is accurate?
options: She must act, since being named executor is a binding contractual duty
She may decline before she starts to act, after weighing her personal risk
She may decline only with court approval, even before she starts to act
She must act, but a trust company will be added to share any liability
questions.explain: Being named executor is an appointment, not a contractual obligation, so it may be declined before the person starts to act. She should weigh her time, ability and potential liabilities; most corporate executors refuse estates tied to such industries. In Quebec, a sole-heir liquidator cannot decline.

questions.q: How does naming a guardian for minor children in a will differ between the common-law provinces and Quebec?
options: Common law: the executor picks the guardian; Quebec: the liquidator acts as tutor
Common law: the choice binds the court; Quebec: the Public Curator approves every tutor
Common law: no court step at all; Quebec: the tutor is homologated after a medical evaluation
Common law: court approval, usually within 90 days; Quebec: no court step unless contested
questions.explain: In common-law provinces the will merely states wishes: the guardian must be approved by court order, usually within 90 days, and the court can overrule the choice. In Quebec, a tutor designated by will, protection mandate or declaration to the Public Curator needs no court step unless contested.

questions.q: A child inherits money under a will that names no trustee. In a common-law province, who manages the funds until the child reaches the age of majority?
options: The executor, until the child turns 30
A public trustee appointed by the court
The child's grandparents, jointly
The surviving parent, automatically
questions.explain: If assets go to minors with no trustee named, the court appoints a public trustee until the age of majority; the surviving parent has no automatic right and must apply to court. In Quebec, by contrast, the surviving parent is automatically tutor and administers the legacy.

questions.q: In Quebec, a trust needs at least one trustee who is not a beneficiary, so a beneficiary cannot act alone as trustee.
options: True
False
questions.explain: True. Right after its Quebec rules on tutorship and trusts for minors, the course notes that a trust requires at least one independent trustee, someone who is not a beneficiary of the trust, so a beneficiary cannot act alone as trustee.

questions.q: Clara's will leaves 'my Muskoka cottage' to her nephew. She later sells the cottage and uses the proceeds to buy a lakeside condo. At her death, what does the nephew receive under that clause?
options: Cash equal to the cottage's sale price, from the estate
A share of the residue equal to the cottage's value
The condo, as replacement property for the cottage
Nothing, because the specific gift has adeemed
questions.explain: A gift of a specific asset the testator no longer owns at death adeems (fails), and the beneficiary gets no replacement even if the proceeds can be traced to new property. Describing gifts in general terms ('my car' rather than 'my Buick') reduces this risk.

questions.q: Under Ontario-style anti-lapse rules, a will leaves '$15,000 to my brother Paul' with no other wording. Paul dies before the testator, leaving a wife and a son. What happens to the $15,000?
options: It lapses and falls into the residue of the testator's estate
It is paid to Paul's estate and passes under Paul's own will
It is divided equally among the testator's other siblings
It goes to Paul's family as if Paul had died intestate
questions.explain: Anti-lapse rules apply when the beneficiary is the testator's child, grandchild, brother or sister and the will shows no contrary intention, so the gift passes to the beneficiary's spouse and children. Adding 'if he survives me' would make it lapse into the residue.

questions.q: Rosa leaves her estate 'to my children in equal shares per stirpes.' Ana and Ben survive her; her third child, Carl, died earlier, leaving two children. How is the estate divided?
options: Ana 1/2 and Ben 1/2, since only surviving children can share
Ana 1/3, Ben 1/3, and Carl's two children share his 1/3 equally
Ana, Ben and each of Carl's two children take one quarter each
Ana 1/3 and Ben 1/3, with Carl's third falling into the residue
questions.explain: Per stirpes means 'by roots': a predeceased child's share is divided equally among his or her children, so Carl's third goes to his two children. A per capita gift (in common law) would be split only between the surviving children, Ana and Ben.

questions.q: In a Quebec succession, what does 'representation' mean?
options: A tutor represents a minor heir until the age of majority
The liquidator represents the heirs in any claim against the estate
A co-legatee takes the share of a legatee who died before the testator
A descendant inherits in place of his or her predeceased parent
questions.explain: Representation lets a descendant inherit in place of a predeceased parent, and where it applies the devolution is always per stirpes (by roots). Taking a co-legatee's share is accretion: e.g., a cottage left to A and B goes entirely to B if A dies first.

questions.q: Victor's will leaves cash legacies of $30,000 to his niece and $10,000 to his nephew, and the residue to his sister. After debts, taxes and expenses, only $20,000 remains. If the legacies abate proportionately, how much does the niece receive?
questions.explain: Debts, taxes and expenses come first, leaving $20,000 against $40,000 of legacies, so each legacy is cut to 50%: the niece gets $15,000, the nephew $5,000 and the residuary sister nothing. Ideally, the will says how any abatement is to be shared.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a 30-day survivorship clause in a will?
options: To give creditors 30 days to file their claims before any assets are distributed
To give the executor 30 days to locate every beneficiary before distributing
To avoid administering the same assets twice if testator and heir die close together
To give a surviving spouse 30 days to choose between the will and a family law property claim
questions.explain: A survivorship clause names an alternate beneficiary if the primary one doesn't survive the testator by a set period (e.g., 30 days), so assets don't pass through two estates after a common accident. The period is short because the beneficiaries are uncertain until it ends.

questions.q: A do-it-yourself will says: 'If my husband Ray survives me by 30 days, I appoint him executor and leave him everything.' What problem does this wording create?
options: Ray has no authority to act as executor for the first 30 days after the death
Ray receives only the estate's income until the 30 days have passed
Ray's gift is void, since a survivorship condition cannot apply to a spouse
The estate must be probated twice, before and after the 30-day period
questions.explain: Making the executor's appointment conditional on surviving 30 days means the spouse is not in charge for those 30 days, which is not what was intended. The survivorship condition should govern who receives the gift, not leave the estate without an executor.

questions.q: Years ago Omar named his sister beneficiary of his life insurance on the insurer's form. His new will names his partner as beneficiary of the policy instead, but he never notifies the insurer. Which statement is accurate?
options: The will's designation is void, because the insurer did not witness the will
The proceeds go to Omar's estate, because the two designations conflict
The will's later designation prevails in law, but the insurer may still pay the sister
The insurer's form prevails, because a will can never change a beneficiary designation
questions.explain: A will can name or revoke a beneficiary of life insurance, an RRSP or a RRIF, and the designation made later prevails in law. But insurers usually pay the beneficiary on file, so a copy of the will (better, a new designation form) should be filed, or costly litigation may follow.

questions.q: Because a will is revocable, a beneficiary designation made in a will cannot be irrevocable.
options: True
False
questions.explain: True. Wills are revocable, so an irrevocable beneficiary designation cannot be made in a will. A revocable designation can be, because even an invalid will (e.g., a formal will with only one witness) counts as a written declaration.

questions.q: Before paying any legacies, what must the executor (liquidator) pay or provide for?
options: Funeral expenses and debts only; taxes are paid out of the residue later
Funeral expenses, probate and legal fees, executor's fees, debts and taxes
The largest specific legacies first, then the debts and the funeral costs
The residue, then debts, taxes and fees out of the remaining legacies
questions.explain: Funeral expenses, probate fees, legal and executor's fees, debts and taxes are paid or provided for before any general or specific legacies. The residue is distributed last, after all fees, taxes, debts and legacies have been settled.

questions.q: In Quebec, how does a (simple) mandate or power of attorney differ from a protection mandate?
options: A simple mandate covers property and ends on incapacity; a protection mandate applies after it
A simple mandate can cover personal care; a protection mandate covers only the person's property
A simple mandate survives the mandator's death; a protection mandate ends at the mandator's death
A simple mandate must be homologated by the court; a protection mandate is effective on signing
questions.explain: A simple mandate (power of attorney) deals only with property, takes effect when the grantor chooses and ends on incapacity or death.
